Open Steam on Linux, pick a game that only ever shipped for Windows, and press Play. A few seconds later the title screen appears and your controller just works. Nothing to see here.
Have you ever stopped to think how remarkable that is? The game was never recompiled for Linux, and the computer never secretly booted Windows. So how is it running?
On Linux, the solution hides in a handful of names that always seem to show up together: Wine, Vulkan, DXVK and Proton. Let’s ride along with the game now, from launch to the first frame, and see where each name makes its entrance.
>_ READING ROUTE
From an .exe to a frame on the screen This article covers only the case where the CPU instruction set matches: an x86-64 game on an x86-64 computer. Running across instruction sets (on an ARM machine, say) needs yet another layer of instruction translation, and that is a story for another day.
We start with why a program depends on its operating system, then see how Wine fills in the Windows environment, take graphics and shaders apart, and finish with Proton and the Steam Deck. The diagram below is the map for the whole trip; come back to it if you get lost.
The same game.exe, with different layers underneath
Windows Linux · Steam + Proton Game game.exe the same file, not recompiled System APIs kernel32.dll user32.dll …shipped with Windows kernel32.dll user32.dll …Wine's reimplementations, same names Proton Graphics API d3d11.dllDirect3D 11 d3d11.dllDXVK: Direct3D outside, Vulkan inside GPU driver Windows driverAMD · NVIDIA · Intel Vulkan driverMesa RADV · NVIDIA … Kernel Windows NT Linux Hardware x86-64 CPU · GPU the same machine identical on bothstand-ins supplied by Proton
A Direct3D 11 game. The game and its CPU instructions stay the same; the layers in between change. The game still loads files named kernel32.dll and d3d11.dll, but receives the Wine and DXVK versions. The CPU understands it. Why can’t the system run it? # Suppose you copy a Windows game’s game.exe straight onto a Linux machine. Both are x86-64, so the CPU understands the machine instructions inside. Does an addition stop being an addition, or a jump stop being a jump, just because the operating system changed?
No. And yet the game still won’t run directly, because a game is more than arithmetic. It has to be loaded into memory and find its libraries; then it opens files, creates windows, reads the controller and sends drawing work to the GPU. All of that relies on agreements between the program and its environment, and game.exe only ever signed those agreements with Windows.
Inside game.exe: which parts does the CPU understand?
▤ game.exe PE32+ · x86-64 PE headersMZ … PE\0\0 entry point · section table · import directory ✕Needs a loader that reads PEThe Linux kernel loads ELF; it does not understand this format.
.textmov eax, [rbx+8] add eax, 1 call [CreateFileW] ✓Runs directly on the CPUx86-64 is x86-64: arithmetic and jumps behave the same. But the call target is not in this file.
Import tableKERNEL32.dll CreateFileW USER32.dll CreateWindowExW d3d11.dll D3D11CreateDevice ✕Needs these DLLs to existand to behave like Windows. The native Linux environment does not supply these Windows DLLs.
Simplified; most sections are omitted. The call in .text reaches CreateFileW through the import table. The CPU can execute the call, but cannot conjure the code it jumps to. Agreement one: how a file becomes a running program # Windows .exe and .dll files use the PE (Portable Executable) format. A header at the start records the entry point, the sections, and which functions to import from which DLLs; the .text section holds machine code and .data holds initialised data. If you want every field, Microsoft’s PE specification has them.
Native Linux programs use ELF. Run ./game.exe in a terminal and the Linux kernel, not recognising the format, will usually just reply Exec format error (unless your system is set up to open .exe files with Wine). Renaming the file won’t help: the contents themselves have a different structure.
Agreement two: who provides system services # Picture a simple scenario. When a game loads a save, it does not touch the disk itself. It calls CreateFileW in kernel32.dll; to open a window, it calls CreateWindowExW in user32.dll. These Windows APIs spell out the rules in detail: how arguments are laid out, how strings are encoded, what comes back on success and which error code is set on failure.
The PE import table says, in effect, “I need CreateFileW from KERNEL32.dll.” Trouble is, the native Linux environment does not supply Windows’ kernel32.dll. And even if it did, Linux’s way of opening files (open, file descriptors, errno) and Windows’ (drive letters, HANDLEs, GetLastError) are two different worlds.
While we are here, it helps to separate an API call from a system call. Here, a Windows API is a function exported by a DLL; a system call is the step into the operating-system kernel. On Windows, CreateFileW passes through ntdll.dll and then into the NT kernel, while plenty of APIs, such as string handling, never touch the kernel at all. Most ordinary games request services through these DLLs. Wine provides compatible interfaces and the required kernel-service behaviour without booting an entire Windows kernel.
Bottom line: executing CPU instructions is only the starting line. What has to be supplied is the entire set of DLLs the game assumes will be there, down to their quirks.
Wine: familiar interfaces in a different environment # Wine began in 1993. Its name expands to Wine Is Not an Emulator. Notice anything? The first word of the expansion is Wine again, so you can keep expanding it forever, like a set of nesting dolls. A name that contains itself is a recursive acronym, a classic open-source joke: GNU stands for GNU’s Not Unix.
The name is more than a joke, though; it describes the approach. When CPU instruction sets differ, an additional emulator or instruction translator is needed. Emulators can also use dynamic compilation rather than interpreting each instruction. In the matching-instruction-set case discussed here, Wine usually needs no translation of ordinary CPU instructions, and the game’s machine code can run directly on the CPU. What Wine does instead is rewrite the Windows DLLs itself: its own kernel32.dll, user32.dll, ntdll.dll, gdi32.dll and so on, with exactly the same names and interfaces as Windows, implemented on top of Linux.
Enough talk. Here is a simplified view of Wine handling one file open, there and back:
Tracing one CreateFileW: the game opens a save
game.exe CreateFileW(L"C:\\Saves\\slot1.sav", GENERIC_READ, …)The game believes it is on Windows: Windows path, Windows API.
Winekernel32 → ntdll C:\Saves\slot1.sav → …/compatdata/<AppID>/pfx/drive_c/saves/slot1.savMap the drive letter to this game's own folder. Windows paths ignore case and Linux paths do not, so Saves must match the saves that actually exists.
wineserver→ Linux kernel openat(…, "…/drive_c/saves/slot1.sav", O_RDONLY) = 23wineserver performs the actual open and gets file descriptor 23 from Linux.
Winewineserver fd 23 ↔ HANDLE 0x1a4Windows programs expect a HANDLE, not an fd. In the same step wineserver allocates a HANDLE that refers to the file, used by later ReadFile and CloseHandle calls.
game.exe hFile = 0x1a4The game receives what looks like an ordinary Windows HANDLE.
Paths follow a Steam Proton prefix; numbers and system calls are conceptual, not an actual trace. The real path also translates access rights, sharing modes and errors: a missing file must come back as Windows' ERROR_FILE_NOT_FOUND, not Linux's ENOENT. One innocent-looking CreateFileW, and Wine already has to deal with drive letters, case sensitivity, mapping file descriptors to HANDLEs, and translating error codes. File objects, sharing modes and other state requiring coordination are managed with the help of wineserver, which plays part of the role of the Windows kernel’s object manager.
Now multiply that by tens of thousands of Windows API functions. Wine has been at it since 1993 and still isn’t done. Worse, programs rely on undocumented behaviour, quirks of particular Windows versions, and sometimes Windows’ own bugs (a mountain of technical debt, you might say), all of which Wine has to faithfully reproduce. It may be one of the most patient projects in software.
Games speak another language: graphics APIs # Great, the window is open. Unfortunately it is also black.
A game engine talks to the GPU through a graphics API: it uploads meshes and textures, sets rendering state, and asks for batches of triangles. Most Windows games speak Direct3D, the 3D part of DirectX, while Linux 3D graphics stacks commonly expose OpenGL and Vulkan.
So on top of the system APIs, the graphics API needs an interpreter too: the game speaks Direct3D, and the compatibility layer has to turn that into something OpenGL or Vulkan understands.
WineD3D: a route through OpenGL # Wine has long had its own interpreter, WineD3D, which implements Direct3D on OpenGL. Many older games first ran on Linux thanks to it, and it is still around: in Proton’s settings, PROTON_USE_WINED3D=1 switches back to it for Direct3D 9 to 11.
The trouble is that the two APIs think differently. The resource management, state objects and multithreading of Direct3D 10 and 11 have no direct equivalent in OpenGL, so WineD3D has to improvise, and shaders must first be turned into GLSL text that the driver then compiles from scratch. When features are hard to map efficiently, the result can be dropped frames or broken rendering. Outcomes still depend on the game, driver and WineD3D version, rather than simply the age of the game.
Vulkan: making GPU work explicit # Then came Vulkan. Khronos revealed it in 2015 and released Vulkan 1.0 on 16 February 2016. Compared with OpenGL, Vulkan hands back to the application many decisions the driver used to make quietly behind the scenes: how memory is allocated, when commands are submitted, how resources are synchronised.
For a compatibility layer, this was huge. All the bookkeeping a Direct3D 11 driver used to do in the background could now be done by the layer itself, on Vulkan, following Direct3D’s rules instead of wrestling with OpenGL’s assumptions. Vulkan still knows nothing about Direct3D, so an interpreter is still needed, but now it has much better tools.
Shaders: graphics calls are only part of the job # Even with every Direct3D call translated to Vulkan, we are only halfway there. Draw calls tell the GPU what to draw; shaders tell it how to compute each vertex and each pixel.
Say a game draws a wall lit by a torch. The mesh and textures are just data, but “where does this vertex land on screen” and “what colour is this pixel in the firelight” are small programs running on the GPU: shaders. A game can contain thousands of them, and Direct3D games commonly ship compiled results from the Direct3D toolchain.
So shaders need translating as well. The diagram below follows a single shader from the moment it is written to the moment it runs on the GPU, and counts the formats it passes through:
The formats one shader passes through
Developer's machine Shipped Player's machine HLSL developer source, usually not shipped ↓ compiled by fxc / dxc DXBC / DXIL bytecode in the game files ↓ translated by DXVK / vkd3d-proton SPIR-V intermediate format for this Vulkan path ↓ compiled by the driver GPU code compiled for the target GPU and driver DXC shortcut · needs source A common path for games shipping precompiled shaders. Without HLSL source, the shortcut is unavailable: the layer starts from DXBC/DXIL, translates to SPIR-V and hands it to the driver. Older D3D8/9 also have other shader formats and fixed-function paths. From HLSL to the bytecode inside a game # For newer programmable shader paths, Windows game shaders are usually written in HLSL and compiled on the developer’s machine with fxc or dxc. What ships with the game is compiled bytecode: DXBC from the older toolchain, DXIL from the newer Direct3D 12 one. In other words, players commonly receive bytecode; the compatibility layer cannot assume the HLSL source is also supplied.
This is the biggest difference between a compatibility layer and a port. A developer porting their own game can consider recompiling HLSL with tools for the target platform, adjusting the code where necessary. Proton faces a released game that may not have been touched in years. For games that ship only precompiled shaders, it must work from that bytecode. It is a bit like translating a printed book into another language when the author’s manuscript is long gone.
(Strictly, DXBC is also the name of a container format, and DXIL is stored inside it; see LLVM’s notes. So “D3D12 means DXIL” is not exact: some Direct3D 12 games still use DXBC.)
Why does Vulkan need SPIR-V? # In the common translation path discussed here, Vulkan receives SPIR-V, rather than DXBC or GLSL source. SPIR-V is a shader intermediate representation defined by Khronos: lower level than source code, but not yet tied to a particular GPU. The driver compiles SPIR-V into its own GPU’s machine code.
The compatibility layer’s job is therefore the highlighted arrow in the diagram: DXBC/DXIL → SPIR-V. Both sides are structured bytecode, so this avoids the extra step of emitting GLSL source for the driver to parse again. Types, resource binding and edge-case behaviour still differ, though, so it is not a dictionary lookup.
Shader and graphics-pipeline compilation are important sources of shader stutter: if compilation remains on the critical path when a frame is needed, that frame can arrive late. Caching and precompilation reduce these stalls but cannot guarantee stutter-free play. Steam’s Shader Pre-Caching uses collected shader and pipeline data to reduce runtime compilation. Fossilize records and replays Vulkan objects so the driver can build a local cache in advance. This is not simply a download of GPU machine code that works unchanged on every system.
An open compiler and translation for existing games # You might be wondering: if there is a tool that compiles HLSL straight to SPIR-V, why not use it? There is one. Microsoft open-sourced the DirectX Shader Compiler (DXC) in 2017. Built on LLVM and Clang, it compiled HLSL to DXIL, and the community later added SPIR-V output. For developers who have the source, DXC is the dashed shortcut in the diagram.
But that DXC compilation path needs source code, which players usually do not have. The road that starts from bytecode still has to be travelled by the translators built into DXVK and vkd3d-proton.
DXVK and vkd3d-proton: connecting graphics to Vulkan # With the targets in place (Vulkan and SPIR-V), it is finally time to meet the two projects that do the actual translating.
DXVK, written by Philip Rebohle, provides d3d9.dll, d3d10core.dll, d3d11.dll, dxgi.dll and related files (plus d3d8.dll since version 2.4). Internally it implements Direct3D 8 to 11 on Vulkan, complete with its own compiler that turns DXBC (and D3D9-era shader bytecode) into SPIR-V. In Proton, D3D8 generally uses Wine’s implementation by default. PROTON_DXVK_D3D8=1 enables DXVK; version and compatibility settings also affect the choice. vkd3d-proton, a fork of Wine’s vkd3d, focuses on Direct3D 12 and turns both DXBC and DXIL into SPIR-V.
The DLL a game loads decides the route
Direct3D 9 – 11 Direct3D 12 Fallback · D3D 9 – 11 Game loads d3d11.dllalso d3d9, dxgi … d3d12.dll  d3d11.dllopt-in only Handled by DXVK vkd3d-proton WineD3D Into Vulkan Vulkan OpenGL Linux graphics driver (Mesa, NVIDIA …) → GPU Proton places the DXVK and vkd3d-proton DLLs in the game's Wine prefix. The game loads d3d11.dll as usual and actually gets DXVK. The route follows the API the game uses; a D3D11 game cannot be sent through vkd3d-proton. The neat part is that the game has no idea it has been swapped. It loads d3d11.dll as usual, calls D3D11CreateDevice, and gets objects that dutifully follow Direct3D 11’s rules, while every call underneath is quietly arranging Vulkan work. It is the same trick Wine plays with kernel32.dll, applied to the graphics layer. The DXVK and vkd3d-proton READMEs describe what each one currently supports.
The graphics components only handle the picture, of course. Files, windows, input and threads are still Wine’s job, and while the game runs the two kinds of calls interleave constantly.
Proton: bringing many projects into one Play button # Wine and later graphics compatibility projects made many Windows games playable on Linux. Before Proton came along, using Wine and the graphics components available at the time often meant a small adventure: install Wine yourself, create a prefix, drop the right DXVK version into it, dig through forums for the mysterious environment variables a particular game needed, and then start over when Wine updated.
Proton folds that whole adventure into a single Steam button. On 21 August 2018 Valve announced a new version of Steam Play that runs Windows games on Linux through Proton. The announcement also mentioned that Valve had brought on the DXVK developer to work on open-source graphics.
What Steam assembles when you press Play
▶ Steam · Play ↓ Steam Linux Runtime a consistent user-space library base Proton each release bundles and tests these together WineWindows APIs, files, windows, threads DXVKDirect3D 9 – 11 → Vulkan vkd3d-protonDirect3D 12 → Vulkan Mediavideo playback through GStreamer Per-game settingsdefaults for known problems Wine prefix compatdata/<AppID>/pfx Each game gets a separate C: drive and registry configuration to reduce interference. Some user directories may still map to the host.
↓ game.exe starts Simplified. The player sees only the button at the top. Steam picks a Proton version for the game, creates the prefix, and starts the game inside the container. Proton itself is a fork of Wine, bundled with DXVK, vkd3d-proton and media components, with each release tested as a whole. Steam creates a separate prefix for every game, reducing the chance that game A’s settings interfere with game B. Newer Proton versions also run inside the Steam Linux Runtime container: this provides a more consistent user-space library base across distributions and makes problems easier to reproduce. GPU drivers and the kernel still depend on the host. The Steam Runtime documentation explains the environment.
None of this is Valve’s work alone. The Wine community has thirty years of implementation behind it; CodeWeavers develops Proton jointly with Valve, with Valve’s funding; and the developers of DXVK, vkd3d-proton and Mesa’s drivers hold down the graphics end.
The Steam Deck puts the stack in a handheld # The Steam Deck, released in February 2022, runs Linux. Its SteamOS 3 is based on Arch Linux; SteamOS 1 and 2 were based on Debian. The full configuration is in the Steam Deck’s specifications.
The Deck brought Proton into a handheld for mainstream players, who could use it every day without needing to know its name. Plenty of people may have owned a Deck for months without realising they were running Linux. Valve added “Deck Verified” ratings, testing games one by one on the Deck and turning compatibility problems into something developers could see and were willing to fix. To check whether a game you want to play works with Proton on Linux, look it up on ProtonDB, where a large number of players report how their games run.
Proton isn’t Deck-exclusive, of course; Steam on any Linux desktop can use it. What makes the Deck special is that hardware, drivers, operating system and Proton can be tuned together, against a small, relatively fixed set of hardware configurations. LCD and OLED models still have hardware differences.
From Wine to the Steam Deck: where the paths meet # Looking back, this is really a story of three tracks: Wine handles the Windows environment, the graphics projects handle drawing and shaders, and Valve integrates components, drivers and the playing experience. They started in different places and ended up meeting at the same one.
Three tracks meeting at the Steam Deck
Windows environment Graphics and shaders Steam integration 1993Wine development begins 2008Wine 1.0 released 2016Vulkan 1.0 (uses SPIR-V) 2018DXVK runs D3D11 games on Vulkan 2018Steam Play adds Proton 2020vkd3d-proton handles D3D12 2022Steam Deck launches Only milestones relevant to this article. Wine and WineD3D supported many games before Vulkan. Vulkan later provided another graphics translation target. Valve integrated Proton in 2018, with vkd3d-proton improving D3D12 support in later releases. Why do some games still fail? # By now you can probably guess: a compatibility layer has to reproduce everything a game actually depends on, not just graphics. The usual sticking points:
Anti-cheat: Easy Anti-Cheat and BattlEye have supported Proton since 2021, but each game’s developer has to flip that switch. Anti-cheat that relies on a Windows kernel driver (scanning memory from inside the kernel) needs a Windows kernel to load its driver into, and there is no Windows kernel underneath Wine, so those solutions are currently unsupported by Proton and need a compatible approach from their vendors. Valve’s Proton developer documentation lists these considerations. Launchers and video: a bundled login launcher, DRM, or cutscenes in an obscure codec can knock a game out before it reaches the main menu. GPU and driver: DXVK and vkd3d-proton require specific Vulkan features. Older cards or drivers that lack them cause trouble, especially for Direct3D 12 games. Updates and regressions: an update to the game, its launcher, the driver or Proton can break a combination that worked perfectly yesterday. Performance has to be judged game by game too. Translation costs some CPU time, and shader or pipeline compilation can cause stutter; yet in some benchmarks, on some hardware, games running through Proton have even beaten Windows. “An extra layer” does not mean “a fixed percentage slower”.
The next time you press Play # Back to that one press, using our Direct3D 11 example. Steam picks a Proton version, prepares the prefix and launches game.exe. The CPU runs the game’s instructions directly; the kernel32.dll the game calls was written by Wine; its d3d11.dll is really DXVK, turning draw commands into Vulkan and shaders into SPIR-V; and the Vulkan driver compiles them and sends them to the GPU. When things go smoothly, the title screen lights up after a few seconds. The compatibility components continue working throughout the game.
And just like that, a game with no Linux release stays in your library, instead of being given up because you switched operating systems.
So next time you press Play on Linux, spare a thought for what is behind that button: Wine, filled in one API at a time since 1993; Vulkan, which finally gave the interpreters decent tools; DXVK and vkd3d-proton, chasing down one game after another; and Valve, which assembled it all into a single button.
If you enjoyed this article, I highly recommend watching SteamDeck 搭载 Linux，凭什么可以玩 Win 游戏？, a Chinese-language video by Redknot-乔红. Watching it is what made me want to write up the technology behind Proton. Technical details and dates were checked against the project documents and original announcements linked throughout; the diagrams are conceptual and leave out some components and calls.
summary: The CPU understands the instructions. Why does the game still need a compatibility layer? Follow Wine, Vulkan and Proton all the way to the Steam Deck.

Useful background: Points in the plane written as complex numbers, and eiθ=cos⁡θ+isin⁡θe^{i\theta} = \cos\theta + i\sin\thetaeiθ=cosθ+isinθ. The rest is built up step by step.
Reading route: Play with the figure first. Then follow one rotating arrow, a sum of arrows, how their sizes are found, and how many are worth keeping.
When the homepage loads, a pen at the end of a chain of spinning circles draws the raven’s outline before the ASCII portrait appears. That animation is a Fourier series: a closed curve written as a sum of rotations. The figure below uses the same coefficients as the homepage. Change the number of circles and watch the outline sharpen.

its radius is ∣c∣|c|∣c∣; its starting angle is the angle of ccc; it completes nnn full turns; positive and negative nnn rotate in opposite directions; with n=0n = 0n=0 it does not move. Arrows placed tip to tail # One arrow can only draw a circle. To draw something more complex, connect several arrows: the second starts at the tip of the first, the third at the tip of the second, and so on.
In the complex plane, placing arrows tip to tail is simply addition: adding two complex numbers joins the arrows that represent them. So the end of the chain is the sum of all the arrows:

This sum is the curve’s Fourier series. Each cnc_ncn​ sets the size and starting angle of one circle.

cn=1N∑k=0N−1zk e−2πink/N.c_n = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} z_k\, e^{-2\pi i n k / N}.cn​=N1​k=0∑N−1​zk​e−2πink/N.This is the discrete Fourier transform (DFT). 2,048 points give 2,048 coefficients, and the fast Fourier transform (FFT) computes them all efficiently. This was done once, when the animation was made; your browser only reads the results.
Which circles to keep # Of the 2,048 possible terms, the homepage keeps 320. The choice is simple: sort by radius ∣cn∣|c_n|∣cn​∣ and keep the largest. The figure’s spectrum shows the same ordering.
The reason comes from Parseval’s theorem. If zKz_KzK​ keeps only some of the terms, the average squared distance between the two curves equals the total squared size of the terms that were dropped:
∫01∣z(t)−zK(t)∣2 dt=∑n dropped∣cn∣2.\int_0^1 \bigl|z(t) - z_K(t)\bigr|^2\, dt = \sum_{n \text{ dropped}} |c_n|^2.∫01​​z(t)−zK​(t)​2dt=n dropped∑​∣cn​∣2.Every dropped term adds its own ∣cn∣2|c_n|^2∣cn​∣2 to the error, and the terms do not interfere with each other. So for a fixed number of circles, keeping the largest ones gives the smallest average squared error. The figure’s RMS and energy readouts are computed directly from this identity.
Compared with the 320-term curve:
Circles Energy kept RMS gap (share of height) 1 86.62% 15.4% 2 91.56% 12.3% 3 95.69% 8.8% 8 99.15% 3.9% 32 99.98% 0.58% 96 > 99.99% 0.16% Energy here means ∑∣cn∣2\sum |c_n|^2∑∣cn​∣2 over the rotating terms. The first eight circles already hold more than 99% of it. The remaining 1% is what separates a blob from a raven.
What the circles find hard # Smooth, gently curving stretches are cheap: low frequencies describe them well. Sharp corners such as the tip of the beak, the claws and the tail are expensive. A corner changes direction suddenly, and only fast-turning arrows can follow that. With few circles every corner is rounded off; more circles make the corners sharper.
That is why the spectrum has a long, slowly shrinking tail. Among the 32 largest terms, the fastest turns 25 times per loop. Among the 96 largest, it turns 68 times. Further down the list, some kept terms turn up to 1,023 times per loop, the highest frequency 2,048 samples can represent. Every term faster than 200 turns, however, has a radius under 0.004% of the raven’s height. They hardly change the picture.
From the formula to the homepage # The same mathematics shaped some engineering choices:
The homepage does not compute the series. A short script, generate_raven_path.py, adds up all 320 terms in advance and stores every point of the 2,048-sample loop as a 16-bit integer pair. The browser only decodes them. The homepage draws at most 96 circles. Circles with a radius under 0.2 pixels cannot be seen. The outline still uses all 320 terms, so skipping tiny circles only simplifies the illustration. This page computes the curve in your browser because you choose the number of circles. Recomputing 2,048 points from up to 320 terms takes no more than a few hundredths of a second. How this website is built describes the site around these pieces.
Circles on circles # Drawing with circles on circles is an old idea. Ancient astronomers described planetary motion with epicycles: a small circle whose centre moves around a larger one. A Fourier series is the same construction with as many circles as needed. Given enough of them, it can follow almost any closed path. That flexibility explains both why epicycles could match observations well and why a good fit alone does not show that a model explains the motion.
The raven on the homepage is not a planet, but the principle is the same: 320 circles, each turning at its own constant speed, are enough to draw it.
summary: A Fourier series explained through the homepage raven: rotating arrows, the discrete Fourier transform, and why keeping the largest circles works.

Building a personal website no longer requires learning web development from scratch first. With a coding agent such as Codex or Claude Code, you can describe your requirements, create pages, adjust layouts, and set up publishing, then refine the result through previews.
Still, “build me a website” leaves many decisions to the tool. Where should articles live? Where will the site be hosted? How will you update it? Does your computer need to stay on?
This article uses the website you are reading as an example. It introduces the main components and their roles, so you can use its architecture as a reference, describe what you want, and work with a coding agent on the implementation.
The big picture: from articles to a website # The basic process is to turn text files and templates into pages, then let a hosting platform serve them to readers.
Articles, images, settings + Blowfish theme ↓ Hugo generates the site ↓ HTML, CSS, JavaScript, images ↓ GitHub Pages / Cloudflare ↓ Reader's browser Component Its role on this site Markdown Holds articles and page content Hugo Combines content, settings, and templates into website files Blowfish Provides the appearance and common reading interfaces Git / GitHub Stores source files and revision history GitHub Actions Automatically builds and publishes updates GitHub Pages Hosts the primary public website Cloudflare Hosts another copy as a mirror Codex / Claude Code Helps connect the components, adjust the design, and check results To begin, you can use Hugo, a theme, and one hosting platform. Publishing to two platforms is a choice made for this site; you do not need both from the start.
Static websites: prepare the pages before readers arrive # A static website has its main page content generated before publication. When someone opens an article, the server sends existing HTML, styles, and images, which the browser displays.
Think of it as a typeset ebook: after adding or editing content, you generate an updated copy and put it online.
This works well for personal profiles, research publications, portfolios, technical notes, and blogs. Their content is usually updated by the author, so there is little need to assemble each page from a database whenever someone visits.
Maintenance is relatively simple, too. This site does not require me to manage a continuously running application and database. Once published, it remains available even when my computer is off.
“Static” does not mean the page cannot move. The galaxy, terminal, and raven interactions on this site run as JavaScript in the browser. Theme switching, expandable content, and article search using a prebuilt index can also work on a static site.
Features that need server-side processing require additional planning: signing users in, storing individual users’ data, or collecting payments, for example. If your main goal is to present your work and write articles, a static website is an approachable starting point.
Hugo: turning content into pages # Hugo is a static site generator. You supply articles, images, settings, and templates; it combines them into a complete website.
Articles are mainly written in Markdown, a text format with simple formatting markers. For example, ## introduces a section heading, and **text** makes text bold. The source remains readable and is easy to work on with a coding agent.
An article might look like this:
--- title: "My first article" date: 2026-10-05 draft: true --- This is the opening paragraph. ## Why build a website? I want somewhere to collect my work and notes. ... The information between the two --- lines is called front matter. It tells Hugo the title, date, and whether the article is a draft. The body follows below.
Hugo also supports multilingual websites. This site’s English and Traditional Chinese pages are written separately and linked through the language switcher. The translations still need to be prepared and checked; Hugo organises them and generates the pages.
For everyday writing, you edit the content while templates take care of navigation, footers, and article layout. As the collection grows, this avoids repeatedly editing the same elements on individual pages.
Blowfish: start with a complete design, then make it your own # Hugo generates the website; the theme supplies its presentation. This site uses Blowfish, a Hugo theme with article layouts, navigation, and light and dark appearances.
A theme gives you a usable site early on. You can add a profile and a few articles, check the structure, and then adjust typography, colours, the homepage, and interactions.
The current homepage includes custom elements such as a research galaxy, a profile panel, and an ASCII raven. These build on the theme: I used Codex to modify HTML templates, CSS, and JavaScript to create the appearance and interactions I wanted.
For example, you could ask:
Use a dark background on the homepage. Show my name, research interests, and contact details first. On mobile, place those details before interactive decorations. Keep article pages quiet and easy to read.
Specific requirements make it easier to judge the preview. Once you can see the result, refine it one change at a time.
GitHub and GitHub Actions: save the content and automate updates # Git records file changes, and GitHub hosts Git repositories. Changes to articles and designs can have a recorded history, making it easier to compare revisions or recover an earlier version.
This site keeps source content and editing history in a private repository. The public repository contains only the generated website files. Readers can access published pages, while drafts, internal notes, and other working files do not have to be published alongside them.
GitHub Actions automates building and publishing. When I push an update to the source repository, GitHub starts a build environment, runs Hugo, and sends the generated files to the hosting platform.
An everyday update therefore becomes: edit an article, preview it locally, push the changes once satisfied, and check that publishing succeeded.
GitHub Pages: giving the website a public address # After generating the files, you need somewhere readers can access them. GitHub Pages is GitHub’s static website hosting service.
Its role differs from the repository: the repository stores files and revisions, while Pages serves website content through a URL. This site’s primary address is https://yenjia.github.io/.
You can start with the address provided by the platform. If you later want your own domain, you can add the domain and DNS configuration. The domain is the address readers enter; the hosting platform supplies the website files.
The initial setup connects Pages with the publishing workflow. A coding agent can help with those settings, but you should still open the production URL after publishing and check the homepage, articles, images, and links.
Cloudflare: hosting the same content on another platform # Cloudflare provides several website and networking services. For static sites, you may encounter Cloudflare Pages or Workers Static Assets. Both can host website files, but their setup and deployment methods differ.
This site’s Cloudflare mirror uses Workers Static Assets. The deployment tool Wrangler uploads the files generated by Hugo. This configuration serves static content without an additional backend program for application logic.
Cloudflare Pages also allows you to upload a prebuilt website. When setting up hosting, identify which service you are using and ask the agent to follow the corresponding documentation.
On this site, GitHub Pages and Cloudflare are independent entry points built and deployed from the same source content. Cloudflare acts as a mirror. It does not sit in front of GitHub Pages, and automatic failover is not configured.
After setup, how do you write the next article? # Once the website is ready, most of your time can go into content. Here, articles live in content/posts/. Add a Markdown file with a title, date, and body, and you have the source for another article.
While writing, keep draft: true so ordinary production builds skip it. Locally, preview with drafts included:
hugo server --buildDrafts This command starts a local preview and prints its URL in the terminal. If a coding agent handles the operation, you do not need to memorize the command. It does not publish the article online. Once the content is ready, change the draft flag to false and use the existing publishing workflow.
For English and Chinese versions, you can follow this site’s naming convention: my-first-post.md and my-first-post.zh-tw.md. Place images in the project’s image directories and reference them from the article. An agent can follow the existing project structure rather than inventing a new arrangement each time.
The initial setup connects the components; later articles reuse that workflow. You can focus on writing and ask the agent for changes when you need a new layout or feature.
How to describe the project to Codex or Claude Code # Once you understand the components, you can give the agent an architecture, content requirements, and completion criteria together. Here is a starting prompt:
Build a personal website with Hugo and Blowfish, including a homepage, an About page, an article list, and research publications. Manage content in Markdown, support English and Traditional Chinese, use a dark appearance, and make it comfortable to read on mobile. Set up GitHub Actions to publish automatically to GitHub Pages. Complete local previews and build checks first, summarize the changes, and wait for my confirmation before publishing. Keep source files in a private repository and publish only generated website files. Store credentials in the platform’s secrets settings.
After the first version, assign another focused task, such as: “Display homepage publications as three cards, stacked in a single column on mobile.” Once the content and appearance are stable, add Cloudflare deployment or more elaborate interactions.
Look at the result after each round: is the text readable, does the mobile page scroll sideways, does language switching work, and are images and links intact? Ask the agent to check keyboard operation for interactive elements and ensure content remains accessible when users request reduced motion.
You do not have to memorize every command, but it helps to know which layer you are changing: content, appearance, or publishing. That makes problems easier to describe and proposed changes easier to understand.
These roles connect to make this website: Markdown holds content, Hugo and the theme generate pages, GitHub records changes, Actions automates builds, and hosting platforms provide public access. Prepare the content you want people to see, choose a simple publishing route, and work with a coding agent on the first version. You can develop it into your own website over time.
summary: Understanding each component makes it easier to describe what you want to a coding agent. This article explains how this site goes from content and design to automated publishing.

What is a sequence model? # A sequence model can be seen as a function that maps one sequence to another, and the Transformer is the classic example. Models of this kind handle many types of problems and data, including text, images, audio and video. For example:
Language models: GPT, Claude, Gemini and others Vision-language models: LLaVA, and LLaVA-Med, which I covered in another article Image models: the many vision transformers Most of these state-of-the-art models are built on Transformers, which means one architecture can handle problems in different modalities. Take LLaVA: an image is encoded into feature vectors by a vision encoder, text is turned into tokens by a tokenizer, and then a single Transformer-based model can classify, or act as a chatbot. ViT does something similar.
Why are Transformers so convenient? # A Transformer block consists of multi-head attention, layer norm, feed forward (MLP), dropout and skip connections. Multi-head attention is the most important part.
A Transformer block (from Build a Large Language Model From Scratch) Once you have a Transformer block, scaling the model up is easy: stack more blocks, or use a Mixture of Experts (MoE, such as Mixtral 8×7B). Model size can be adjusted to whatever you need. This simplicity is one reason Transformer-based models became so popular.
Scaling laws # Transformers also come with an important rule of thumb, scaling laws. These are empirical observations that let you predict a model’s performance before training, from the dataset size, total compute and model size.
DeepMind’s Chinchilla scaling law is one of the best known. Here LLL can be read as the loss, NNN is the number of model parameters, and DDD is the number of training tokens:
L(N,D)=E+AN0.34+BD0.28,E=1.69, A=406.4, B=410.7L(N, D) = E + \frac{A}{N^{0.34}} + \frac{B}{D^{0.28}}, \quad E = 1.69,\ A = 406.4,\ B = 410.7L(N,D)=E+N0.34A​+D0.28B​,E=1.69, A=406.4, B=410.7Its main conclusion is that for a fixed compute budget, model size and the number of training tokens should be scaled in equal proportion, at roughly 20 training tokens per parameter. In other words, growing the model and the data together should lower the loss. The figure below is from OpenAI’s earlier scaling-law study: test loss falls steadily as compute, data and parameters increase.
Figure 1 from Kaplan et al. (2020) The limits of Transformers # Transformers have proved powerful across many applications, and their performance improves readily with more resources. But there is a problem: because of attention, the computation grows quadratically with the context length. So the number of input and output tokens is capped, and they are hard to apply directly to long sequences such as video.
There are two mainstream answers for long sequences:
Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) works like an extension: it retrieves data from an external database and gives a tailored answer. It’s like being allowed a cheat sheet in an exam. You have to organize and condense the information onto the sheet beforehand so you can find what you need during the exam. A larger context window lets the model read more tokens at once, for example a context window of a million tokens. Either way, it is better to cut the computation so that replies over long sequences come faster. Mamba is designed to handle long sequences efficiently in both training and inference.
State space models # Before Mamba, we need to meet its predecessors. We start with the state space model (SSM), which comes from control theory and describes a dynamic system with differential equations:
x′(t)=Ax(t)+Bu(t)y(t)=Cx(t)+Du(t)\begin{aligned} x'(t) &= Ax(t) + Bu(t) \\ y(t) &= Cx(t) + Du(t) \end{aligned}x′(t)y(t)​=Ax(t)+Bu(t)=Cx(t)+Du(t)​Here u(t)u(t)u(t) is the input signal, x(t)x(t)x(t) is the state, and y(t)y(t)y(t) is the output. AAA is the state matrix, which multiplies the state; BBB and CCC are the input and output matrices; DDD acts like a skip connection and is usually set to 0 to drop the term.
Block diagram of a state space model The idea of an SSM is to remember past information in a smaller state, a bit like an RNN. That is how it handles long sequences.
Discretization: the recurrent and convolutional views # The most important step in an SSM is discretization, because it determines how efficient training and inference are. After discretization, the continuous system can be turned into two views.
The first is the recurrent view. Discretizing with the trapezoid (bilinear) method and a step size Δ\DeltaΔ turns the system into a recurrence:
xk=Aˉxk−1+Bˉuk,Aˉ=(I−Δ2A)−1(I+Δ2A)yk=Cˉxk,Bˉ=(I−Δ2A)−1ΔB,Cˉ=C\begin{aligned} x_k &= \bar{A}x_{k-1} + \bar{B}u_k, & \bar{A} &= (I - \tfrac{\Delta}{2}A)^{-1}(I + \tfrac{\Delta}{2}A) \\ y_k &= \bar{C}x_k, & \bar{B} &= (I - \tfrac{\Delta}{2}A)^{-1}\Delta B, \quad \bar{C} = C \end{aligned}xk​yk​​=Aˉxk−1​+Bˉuk​,=Cˉxk​,​AˉBˉ​=(I−2Δ​A)−1(I+2Δ​A)=(I−2Δ​A)−1ΔB,Cˉ=C​At inference time we can generate outputs with this formula. The next output depends only on the current state and the current input, so inference is very efficient, just like an RNN.
The second is the convolutional view. Unrolling the recurrence writes the output as a convolution of the input with a kernel:
y=Kˉ∗u,Kˉ=(CˉBˉ, CˉAˉBˉ, …, CˉAˉL−1Bˉ)y = \bar{K} \ast u, \qquad \bar{K} = (\bar{C}\bar{B},\ \bar{C}\bar{A}\bar{B},\ \dots,\ \bar{C}\bar{A}^{L-1}\bar{B})y=Kˉ∗u,Kˉ=(CˉBˉ, CˉAˉBˉ, …, CˉAˉL−1Bˉ)During training the whole sequence is known, so the convolution can be computed in parallel. This is where SSMs differ from RNNs, which must be trained one step at a time.
The matrix A and HiPPO # In an SSM, BBB and CCC are learnable, and the choice of AAA is crucial. The convolution kernel needs Aˉk\bar{A}^kAˉk, which is still expensive, so AAA should ideally be a normal matrix: normal matrices are unitarily diagonalizable, which makes powers easy to compute.
SSMs also initialize AAA with the HiPPO (High-Order Polynomial Projection Operator) matrix. The HiPPO matrix is derived from a specific measure and helps the state remember earlier information; the proofs and experiments are in an earlier paper by the same author. The version used in S4 (HiPPO-LegS) is:
Ank=−{2n+1 2k+1n>kn+1n=k0n<kA_{nk} = -\begin{cases} \sqrt{2n+1}\,\sqrt{2k+1} & n > k \\ n + 1 & n = k \\ 0 & n < k \end{cases}Ank​=−⎩⎨⎧​2n+1​2k+1​n+10​n>kn=kn<k​This matrix is not normal, though. The authors decompose it into a normal matrix plus a low-rank matrix, then use their algorithm to speed up both the recurrent and the convolutional computation. Empirically, SSMs initialized with HiPPO perform well, but not when AAA is initialized randomly.
Structured state space models (S4) # Put all this together and you get S4:
S4 = SSM + HiPPO + Structured matrices
That is, use a state space model, replace AAA with the HiPPO matrix, and learn the parameters with structured matrices and a dedicated algorithm.
Three aspects of S4 (from Albert Gu’s talk) S4 has some useful properties:
Resolution invariance: because the model comes from a continuous system, it can be trained on low-resolution data and used on high-resolution data. This is especially handy for audio, where lowering the sample rate speeds up training. Efficient training: training can use the convolution and run in parallel. Efficient inference: inference can use the recurrence. Mamba # Mamba: Linear-Time Sequence Modeling with Selective State Spaces by Albert Gu and Tri Dao (code on GitHub) sets out to solve the problems that attention brings. It adds two improvements on top of SSMs:
A selective mechanism, which lets the model decide, based on the input, what to focus on or ignore. A hardware-aware algorithm, which designs the computation around the GPU’s memory hierarchy. According to the paper, Mamba reaches 5× higher inference throughput than Transformers and state-of-the-art results across modalities such as language, audio and genomics. It is also the first attention-free model to match Transformer performance: Mamba-3B outperforms Transformers of the same size.
Notation and discretization # The Mamba paper uses slightly different notation: hhh is the state, xxx the input, and yyy the output. The continuous and discretized systems are:
h′(t)=Ah(t)+Bx(t)ht=Aˉht−1+Bˉxty(t)=Ch(t)yt=Cht\begin{aligned} h'(t) &= Ah(t) + Bx(t) & \qquad h_t &= \bar{A}h_{t-1} + \bar{B}x_t \\ y(t) &= Ch(t) & \qquad y_t &= Ch_t \end{aligned}h′(t)y(t)​=Ah(t)+Bx(t)=Ch(t)​ht​yt​​=Aˉht−1​+Bˉxt​=Cht​​Here the discretization is the zero-order hold (ZOH):
Aˉ=exp⁡(ΔA),Bˉ=(ΔA)−1(exp⁡(ΔA)−I)⋅ΔB\bar{A} = \exp(\Delta A), \qquad \bar{B} = (\Delta A)^{-1}\left(\exp(\Delta A) - I\right) \cdot \Delta BAˉ=exp(ΔA),Bˉ=(ΔA)−1(exp(ΔA)−I)⋅ΔBDiscretization is deeply tied to the continuous-time system, which gives the model extra properties such as resolution invariance and keeps it properly normalized. The figure below shows the state space model inside Mamba. The orange part is the state; AAA extracts features and information from the state, and BBB and CCC handle the input and output.
Selective state space model (Figure 1 of the Mamba paper) The first improvement: the selective mechanism # In S4, AAA, BBB, CCC and Δ\DeltaΔ don’t depend on the input; the model is time-invariant. Mamba makes BBB, CCC and Δ\DeltaΔ depend on the input by adding the sequence length LLL as a dimension in the algorithm, so the model becomes time-varying:
S4 and S6, which adds selection (Algorithms 1 and 2 of the Mamba paper) where:
sB(x)=LinearN(x)sC(x)=LinearN(x)sΔ(x)=BroadcastD(Linear1(x))τΔ=softplus\begin{aligned} s_B(x) &= \mathrm{Linear}_N(x) \\ s_C(x) &= \mathrm{Linear}_N(x) \\ s_\Delta(x) &= \mathrm{Broadcast}_D(\mathrm{Linear}_1(x)) \\ \tau_\Delta &= \mathrm{softplus} \end{aligned}sB​(x)sC​(x)sΔ​(x)τΔ​​=LinearN​(x)=LinearN​(x)=BroadcastD​(Linear1​(x))=softplus​sBs_BsB​, sCs_CsC​ and sΔs_\DeltasΔ​ are linear layers, τΔ\tau_\DeltaτΔ​ is softplus (a smooth approximation of ReLU), and the selective mechanism lives mainly in sΔs_\DeltasΔ​ and τΔ\tau_\DeltaτΔ​.
The selective mechanism is related to gating in RNNs. Theorem 1 of the paper looks at a special case: when N=1N = 1N=1, A=−1A = -1A=−1, B=1B = 1B=1, sΔ=Linear(x)s_\Delta = \mathrm{Linear}(x)sΔ​=Linear(x) and τΔ=softplus\tau_\Delta = \mathrm{softplus}τΔ​=softplus, the selective SSM recurrence becomes:
gt=σ(Linear(xt))ht=(1−gt) ht−1+gt xt\begin{aligned} g_t &= \sigma(\mathrm{Linear}(x_t)) \\ h_t &= (1 - g_t)\,h_{t-1} + g_t\,x_t \end{aligned}gt​ht​​=σ(Linear(xt​))=(1−gt​)ht−1​+gt​xt​​This is very similar to the forget gate in an RNN: a gate decides what to keep, the past state or the current input. The proof is in the paper’s appendix.
The second improvement: a hardware-aware algorithm # Once the selective mechanism is added, Aˉ\bar{A}Aˉ and Bˉ\bar{B}Bˉ change over time, so the model can no longer be trained as a convolution. The authors solve this with three classic techniques:
Kernel fusion Parallel scan Recomputation Parallel scan is the most important; it is also used to compute linear RNNs. The real bottleneck is not the arithmetic but the I/O between two kinds of GPU memory: HBM (High Bandwidth Memory) and SRAM (Static Random-Access Memory), and SRAM is much faster than HBM. The main idea is to compute the key steps, discretization and the scan, in SRAM to reduce I/O.
Mamba’s architecture # H3 is one branch of SSM work. Mamba combines H3 with a gated MLP into a single Mamba block; the gated MLP is often used as an alternative to self-attention with fewer parameters. Mamba blocks can be stacked just like Transformer blocks.
The Mamba block (Figure 3 of the Mamba paper) Results # The first experiment covers scaling laws on The Pile with models from 125M to 1.3B parameters. Mamba follows scaling laws just like Transformers do, with similar results at longer sequence lengths.
Scaling laws (Figure 4 of the Mamba paper) The second is efficiency. Thanks to the hardware-aware algorithm, Mamba’s scan is faster than both FlashAttention-2 and convolution, which gives Mamba higher inference throughput, about five times that of a Transformer.
Efficiency benchmarks (Figure 8 of the Mamba paper) Conclusion # Mamba starts from state space models, uses HiPPO and S4 to lay the groundwork for remembering long sequences and computing efficiently, adds a selective mechanism so the model can choose what to remember based on content, and wins back efficiency with a hardware-aware algorithm.
For me, the most interesting thing about this paper is that it offers a path beyond attention. Attention-free sequence models are worth following, worth trying for training and inference, and could even be used to build foundation models.
References # Albert Gu and Tri Dao. Mamba: Linear-Time Sequence Modeling with Selective State Spaces. arXiv preprint arXiv:2312.00752, 2023. Albert Gu, Karan Goel, and Christopher Ré. Efficiently Modeling Long Sequences with Structured State Spaces. arXiv preprint arXiv:2111.00396, 2021. Jordan Hoffmann et al. Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models. arXiv preprint arXiv:2203.15556, 2022. Jared Kaplan et al. Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models. arXiv preprint arXiv:2001.08361, 2020. Haotian Liu, Chunyuan Li, Qingyang Wu, and Yong Jae Lee. Visual Instruction Tuning. Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems, 2023. Alexey Dosovitskiy et al. An Image is Worth 16x16 Words: Transformers for Image Recognition at Scale. arXiv preprint arXiv:2010.11929, 2020. Sebastian Raschka. Build a Large Language Model From Scratch. Loïck Bourdois. Introduction to State Space Models (SSM). Albert Gu’s talk on S4, 2022.
summary: Attention grows quadratically with length. How does Mamba remember the past in a small state and still train and run fast?
title: Sequence models without attention: from state space models to Mamba

>_ BEFORE YOU READ
What question does this article answer? Core question: How can existing vision and language models be adapted into a conversational model that answers questions about medical images?
Useful background: A basic understanding of encoders, embeddings, and fine-tuning is enough; prior reading of LLaVA is optional.
Reading route: Follow the data construction, the two training stages, and then the evaluation methods. Notice how GPT-4 generates training conversations without seeing the images.
This reading note covers the original 2023 paper and was published in February 2024. Descriptions of models and tools should be read in that historical context.
Deep learning has shown promising performance on a range of medical tasks. In classification, for example, physicians can combine model outputs with their own experience to inform diagnosis. Yet many common models produce just one output for an image, such as classification logits or a segmentation mask.
A medical image can contain much more information. Some findings may relate to the target task without being its main focus—for example, an organ may show inflammation rather than a malignant tumor. Others may be unrelated to the original question but still warrant follow-up. Microsoft’s LLaVA-Med: Training a large language-and-vision assistant for biomedicine in one day, published in 2023, combines language and vision to help describe the contents of medical images.
LLaVA-Med is a conversational vision-language model. Given an image, users can ask questions or request a description, much like chatting with ChatGPT. General-purpose multimodal models available at the time of this article, such as Google Bard, could also process images and text, but their answers could be unreliable because they lacked specialized medical knowledge. This paper presents an efficient training approach that adapts existing open-source models using medical data, reporting promising results after 15 hours of training on eight 40 GB A100 GPUs.
Features and contributions # The main features and contributions can be summarised as follows:
A large, diverse dataset of medical figure-caption pairs. Open-ended instruction-following data generated with GPT-4. Two-stage training: biomedical concept alignment followed by end-to-end instruction tuning. Affordable development costs and an approach that can transfer to other domains. Low-cost serving, with inference possible on consumer GPUs. Biomedical visual instruction-following data # The two training stages require different datasets. The source is PMC-15M, a collection of 15 million image-text pairs extracted from PubMed Central. Each pair contains an image and its corresponding caption.
For stage 1, the authors randomly sample 600,000 pairs to help align visual and language representations with biomedical concepts. They call this biomedical concept alignment data. Training uses single-turn instructions, as illustrated below.
Here, X_q denotes the question, X_v the image, and X_c its caption. The model describes the image using either a brief description or a detailed description.
For stage 2, the authors sample 60,000 pairs and prepare multi-turn conversations. The images cover five modalities: chest X-rays, CT, MRI, histopathology, and gross pathology. Because the source dataset does not include multi-turn image-based conversations, GPT-4 generates them from the captions.
Crucially, GPT-4 did not see the images in this process. It received captions and prompts asking it to respond as though it could see the image, generating two or three turns of questions and answers from a visual perspective. Figure 4 illustrates this procedure. The resulting dataset is called biomedical instruction-tuning data.
Training approach # Training has two stages. Biomedical concept alignment runs for one epoch, followed by three epochs of end-to-end instruction tuning, as shown in Figure 3. Additional fine-tuning can then be performed for downstream tasks.
The approach does not depend on a special architectural trick and can be applied to other vision-language architectures. In stage 1, the model predicts image captions while the image encoder and language model remain frozen. Only the projection matrix after the image encoder is updated, with the aim of aligning visual concepts with word embeddings.
In stage 2, the language model also participates in training using the GPT-4-generated multi-turn conversations. The authors report strong zero-shot performance on some visual question answering (VQA) datasets after this stage.
Experimental results # The authors evaluate the medical chatbot in two ways. First, they construct a validation set of 193 questions, including conversations and detailed image descriptions, and use GPT-4 to score the responses. Table 1 compares LLaVA-Med with LLaVA, a model trained only on stage 1, and models trained with different amounts of data. Even with 10,000 examples, LLaVA-Med outperforms LLaVA in this evaluation, and additional data further improves performance.
The second evaluation uses three medical VQA datasets:
VQA-RAD: 315 radiology images and 3,515 question-answer pairs generated by clinicians. SLAKE (Semantically-Labeled Knowledge-Enhanced dataset for medical VQA): 642 radiology images and more than 7,000 question-answer pairs created by experienced physicians. PathVQA: 4,998 pathology images and 32,799 question-answer pairs. Questions are divided into open-ended and closed-ended categories. Open-ended answers are evaluated by the proportion of ground-truth tokens appearing in the generated answer; closed-ended answers are evaluated using accuracy. Table 3 shows promising results for LLaVA-Med in both categories.
Together with the paper’s ablation studies, these experiments suggest two main points:
Longer stage 1 training improves zero-shot transfer, but stage 1 alone is insufficient. Instruction-following data is crucial for stage 2. An additional case study # Although the training conversations use only English, the model demonstrates an ability to answer Chinese questions in the example shown in Table 6. The authors speculate that LLaMA may already have acquired some multilingual knowledge, making this transfer possible. Other existing models may not transfer to a different language as successfully in a zero-shot setting.
Conclusion # LLaVA-Med is a large vision-language model focused on biomedicine. GPT-4 is used to create medical visual instruction-following data. After further fine-tuning, LLaVA-Med surpasses other models on some evaluation metrics. It still exhibits familiar limitations of large language models, including hallucinations and limited deep reasoning. ↳ TAKEAWAYS
Three ideas and a follow-up question Data construction is part of the method: Figure-caption pairs and GPT-4-generated conversations serve different training stages. The stages have different purposes: First align visual and language representations, then learn to follow biomedical instructions. Evaluation methods shape the interpretation: GPT-4 scores, answer-token coverage, and closed-ended accuracy measure different aspects of performance. A follow-up question: Which information in an image can caption-generated conversations capture, and which information might they miss?
Scope of the evidence: Read the reported evaluations and Chinese-language example alongside the model’s hallucinations and reasoning limitations.
For further reading, start with the original paper and official code linked below.
References # Li, Chunyuan, Cliff Wong, Sheng Zhang, Naoto Usuyama, Haotian Liu, Jianwei Yang, Tristan Naumann, Hoifung Poon, and Jianfeng Gao. “LLaVA-Med: Training a large language-and-vision assistant for biomedicine in one day.” arXiv preprint arXiv:2306.00890 (2023). In 2023, when everyone is focused on LLMs, here is an image visualization method that has received little attention but works well. For image classification, many people use visualization to explain what a model bases its decision on. The method in this article builds on one idea, the Information Bottleneck, to create an alternative to gradient-based methods such as Grad-CAM. The paper shows that it comes with some theoretical guarantees and can easily be applied to all kinds of model architectures. This article aims for an intuitive understanding rather than a detailed derivation.
Introduction # Restricting the Flow: Information Bottlenecks for Attribution, published at ICLR 2020, is the paper we will discuss. Work on visualization and interpretability often runs into a few hard problems, for example:
Methods are hard to apply to unusual, custom model architectures. Some methods are slow and inefficient (Occlusion Sensitivity, for instance). Gradient-based methods are sensitive to model parameters and tend to include unimportant regions. To get precise results, the authors bring in the Information Bottleneck. Backed by information theory, it guarantees that regions of an image judged irrelevant are not necessary for the model’s prediction.
What is the Information Bottleneck? # Information Bottleneck The Information Bottleneck is this one expression, first proposed in 2000, where I denotes mutual information. Put simply, the goal is to maximize the mutual information between Y and Z while minimizing (hence the minus sign) the mutual information between X and Z. β is a manually tuned parameter.
That may still not make clear what X, Y and Z mean here, so let’s map the idea onto a familiar model. The blue boxes are one complete model (ResNet50, say), split into a front and a back half. X is the input, Z is the intermediate result after X passes through the front half, that is, the features, and Y is the output. Back to the expression: minimizing the information between X and Z means filtering out as much unimportant information as possible (such as an image’s background) and keeping the important information Z, which is the idea of feature extraction. The remaining features must still classify well, so we also maximize the information between Y and Z, which is what an ordinary classification model already does.
You might notice that the whole process resembles compression and decompression. When compressing, we want a high compression ratio without losing too much of the file (for lossy compression).
Architecture # Per-Sample Bottleneck The paper proposes two architectures. Since they share the main idea, I’ll introduce the first one, the Per-Sample Bottleneck. First, the model is split into two parts, “net-” and “-work” in the figure. R is the features obtained after the input passes through the front half. α is a trainable mask. λ is the result of applying the sigmoid function to α, and ε is noise drawn from a Gaussian distribution. Z is a weighted average of R and the noise, weighted by λ according to the mask.
The core idea is to add noise to the features, using the mask to control which positions are replaced with noise, and then feed the noisy features into the back half to get the output. We learn the mask with the Information Bottleneck objective, so that it finds which positions can be replaced with noise without affecting the final prediction. Finally, α gives us the heatmap for the image.
Results # Figure 8 from reference 1 Figure 4 from reference 2 Besides the paper’s own results, I’ve added results on medical images. Overall, compared with the familiar Grad-CAM, Grad-CAM more often highlights unimportant regions and its results tend to blur together, and the same problem appears in the medical imaging examples. Still, neither visualization methods nor models are perfect, so use them with care.
Conclusion # This article introduced the paper as simply and intuitively as possible, covering:
The Information Bottleneck How the Information Bottleneck can be applied to visualization The idea can be applied to other problems and needs too, such as the compression mentioned above. The authors of this paper approached it from visualization and the structure of classification models, designed a method around the concept, and achieved good results.
References # Karl Schulz, Leon Sixt, Federico Tombari, & Tim Landgraf (2020). Restricting the Flow: Information Bottlenecks for Attribution. In International Conference on Learning Representations. Demir, Ugur, et al. “Information bottleneck attribution for visual explanations of diagnosis and prognosis.” Machine Learning in Medical Imaging: 12th International Workshop, MLMI 2021, Held in Conjunction with MICCAI 2021, Strasbourg, France, September 27, 2021, Proceedings 12. Springer International Publishing, 2021. Naftali Tishby, Fernando C Pereira, and William Bialek. The information bottleneck method. arXiv preprint physics/0004057, 2000.
summary: Unlike gradient-based methods such as Grad-CAM, the Information Bottleneck finds the regions of an image a model actually needs.
title: Information Bottleneck: visual, interpretable explanations for classification models
